text: Brightfield Retail is a fictional mid-sized e-commerce company, and this case study walks a realistic composite incident through every chapter of this course, to show how a single offboarding gap cascades into a real breach.

A short-term contractor was hired to build a sales dashboard. Their access was granted broadly, just give them what the analytics team has, instead of scoped to the dashboard work. When the contract ended, payroll and badge access were revoked, but the database login never was, because no single system owned remove database access as a step.

It took gaps in four different chapters lining up at once. Classification, the customer_orders table had never been run through the classification process, so nothing signaled this needs tighter controls. Access control, access was granted by role-copying instead of least privilege, with no segregation-of-duties check and no access review that would have caught the still-active login. Protecting data, the payment-card fragment and shipping addresses weren't masked, and row-level security could have limited queries to aggregated totals instead of individual rows.

Three months later, security noticed the dormant login during an unrelated access review, exactly the kind of catch a periodic review and a well-formed audit log are supposed to enable. The breach response lifecycle kicked in, revoke the login, assess from the audit trail exactly which rows were queried, legal determined notification was required, and affected customers submitted data subject requests once notified.

The actual fix wasn't a new tool, it was closing the gap between systems, a named owner for database offboarding, quarterly access reviews, and row-level security so a reporting login can never see unaggregated rows again. Every control in this course is cheap compared to investigating an incident that forces you to answer all of them at once, under time pressure, with lawyers already involved.
